decision.summary: The tenant's report of a rotten-egg smell from the gas boiler is a possible gas leak and an emergency, not routine, even though she said "not urgent". I opened emergency job JOB-101, sent the tenant safety instructions (leave, no switches or flames, call 0800 111 999), emailed the landlord, texted HeatRight Ltd for urgent attendance, and escalated P1 (ESC-105) because no engineer time is confirmed.

answers.question: 1. What severity is this and why, given the tenant says it is "not urgent"?
answers.answer: Emergency. A rotten-egg smell from a gas appliance is the standard sign of a gas leak (mercaptan odour). Safety rules apply regardless of the tenant's wording. An 82-year-old is also staying at the flat.

answers.question: 2. What exactly do you tell the tenant right now, and in what order?
answers.answer: First: leave the flat now with everyone else, open windows if safe to do so, and don't touch switches, the doorbell, lighters, flames or electrical appliances. Second: once outside, call the National Gas Emergency line on 0800 111 999. Third: don't re-enter until the engineer or emergency line says it is safe, and reply on WhatsApp once out. Then say an urgent engineer visit is being arranged and that a confirmed time will follow.

answers.question: 3. Which actions do you take tonight (job, contractor, escalation, landlord)?
answers.answer: Job JOB-101 created as emergency gas. Tenant WhatsApp with safety steps (A2). Landlord emailed about the report and the spend rule (A3). HeatRight Ltd (C-11, the landlord's preferred boiler contractor, out of hours) texted for urgent attendance (A4). P1 escalation to maintenance (ESC-105) to secure the attendance and a backup contractor. The £300 limit still applies to any repair after make-safe.

Hi Amelia, thanks for telling us. A rotten egg smell from a boiler can mean a gas leak, so please treat this as an emergency tonight, even though it's late:
1. Open the windows and leave the flat now, taking your flatmate and her mum with you.
2. Don't touch light switches, the doorbell, lighters or any flames, and don't use electrical appliances.
3. Once you're outside, call the National Gas Emergency line on 0800 111 999 (free, 24 hours).
Please don't go back in until the gas engineer or the emergency line says it's safe. Reply here once you're safe. We're arranging an urgent gas engineer visit and will update you as soon as we have a confirmed time.
